set.detail: In 468 Leo I and the western emperor Anthemius, whom Leo had sent to Italy in 467, launched a combined assault on the Vandal kingdom, the most ambitious military undertaking of the fifth century. Three forces converged on Africa: Marcellinus, the independent ruler of Dalmatia, cleared Sardinia of Vandals; Heraclius of Edessa landed in Tripolitania and advanced overland; and the main fleet under Leo's brother-in-law Basiliscus sailed from Constantinople. John Lydus, a well-placed official, says the expedition cost 65,000 lb of gold and 700,000 lb of silver, an amount that crippled the eastern treasury for years; Procopius speaks of 100,000 men and over 1,100 ships, figures that should not be taken literally. Basiliscus anchored off Promunturium Mercurii (Cape Bon), some 60 km from Carthage, and instead of attacking at once granted Gaiseric's request for a five-day truce to consider terms. Gaiseric used the time to prepare fireships and wait for a favourable wind. When it came, the Vandals towed burning hulks into the crowded Roman fleet at night, and in the confusion attacked with their warships. Much of the fleet was burned or sunk; the general John, rather than be captured by Gaiseric's son Genso, leapt into the sea in full armour. Basiliscus fled to Sicily and returned to Constantinople, where he took sanctuary in Hagia Sophia; Procopius alleges that Aspar had bribed him to fail, so that Leo's power would not be strengthened. Marcellinus was murdered in Sicily soon afterwards, possibly at Ricimer's instigation. The disaster ended the last realistic chance of recovering Africa for the West and with it the fiscal base on which a revived western empire might have rested. In 474 Zeno concluded the 'endless peace' with Gaiseric.
set.debate: Procopius's figures for the fleet are exaggerated; John Lydus's cost figures, though precise, may also be inflated. Aspar's alleged sabotage is uncertain.

scholarship: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

set.detail: In 475 the patrician Orestes, a Roman from Pannonia who had been Attila's secretary and then a general in Italy, drove the emperor Julius Nepos from Ravenna to Dalmatia and on 31 October proclaimed his own young son Romulus emperor. Orestes's power rested on the federate troops of the Italian army, Heruli, Sciri, Rugi and Turcilingi, many of whom had come from the former Hunnic empire. In 476 they demanded land, a third of the estates of Italy according to Procopius, under the system that had been applied to federates in Gaul. Orestes refused. The soldiers turned to Odoacer, son of Edeco (perhaps the Edeco of the embassy of 449) and a former officer of Anthemius's guard, who promised them what they asked. Proclaimed king by the troops on 23 August 476, Odoacer marched against Orestes, who took refuge in Ticinum (Pavia); the city was taken and sacked, and Orestes fled to Placentia, where he was captured and executed on 28 August 476. His brother Paulus was killed at Ravenna, in the Pineta near Classe, on 4 September. Odoacer then entered Ravenna and deposed Romulus. The episode was thus a mutiny of the federate army over the terms of its maintenance, not a barbarian invasion. Odoacer's settlement of his followers, apparently by allocating a third of land or of tax revenues, was carried out by the Roman praetorian prefect Liberius's predecessors and continued by Theodoric. The battle and its aftermath are recorded mostly in brief annals, the Fasti Vindobonenses and the Anonymus Valesianus, which give precise dates; later narrative sources such as Procopius and Jordanes provide the land claim and the background.

scholarship: Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)

set.detail: After defeating Orestes, Odoacer entered Ravenna on 4 September 476 and deposed his son Romulus, whom contemporaries mockingly called Augustulus, the little Augustus. The Anonymus Valesianus says Odoacer spared him because of his youth and beauty, gave him an annual pension of 6,000 solidi, and sent him to live with his relatives in Campania, at the Castellum Lucullanum on the bay of Naples, where a letter of Cassiodorus may show him alive in 507-511. Odoacer did not take the imperial title. Malchus records that the Roman Senate sent an embassy to Zeno saying that one emperor was enough for both parts and that Odoacer, a man of political and military skill, should govern Italy with the title of patricius; the imperial insignia were returned to Constantinople. At the same time Julius Nepos, deposed in 475 but still recognised by Zeno, sent his own envoys from Dalmatia; Zeno told the senators that they should take back Nepos, and Odoacer struck coins in Nepos's name until his murder in 480. Marcellinus Comes, writing in Constantinople around 518, made 476 the end of the western empire: 'the western empire of the Roman people, which Octavian Augustus first began to rule in the 709th year from the foundation of the city, perished with this Augustulus'. Jordanes and later Procopius echoed this. For contemporaries in Italy the change was less dramatic: the Senate, the consulship, the prefecture and the Roman administration continued under Odoacer and Theodoric. Modern historians debate whether 476 marks a real break, as Heather and Ward-Perkins argue in terms of the end of the western state, or merely a symbolic one in a long transformation, as the 'late antiquity' school maintains.
set.debate: Whether the 'Romulus' of Cassiodorus Variae 3.35 is the former emperor is uncertain.

scholarship: Croke, 'AD 476: the manufacture of a turning point', Chiron 13 (1983)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)

set.detail: After the death of Aegidius in 465, his son Syagrius ruled a remnant of Roman Gaul between the Somme and the Loire from Soissons, styled by Gregory of Tours 'king of the Romans', a title probably given to him by the Franks. Clovis, who had succeeded his father Childeric as king of the Salian Franks of Tournai in 481 or 482, challenged him in 486 or 487, together with his relative Ragnachar of Cambrai. Gregory, writing a century later, says simply that Clovis defeated Syagrius in battle and that Syagrius fled to Alaric II at Toulouse; Clovis demanded his surrender, and the Visigoths, fearing the Franks, handed him over in chains. Clovis had him secretly killed. The famous story of the vase of Soissons belongs to the aftermath: Clovis asked his warriors to give him a precious vessel from a church, which he had promised to return to the bishop, Remigius; one warrior struck it with his axe, saying the king should only receive his share by lot. A year later Clovis split the man's skull at a review with the words 'thus you did to the vase at Soissons'. The battle gave Clovis control of northern Gaul as far as the Seine and later the Loire, with its Roman administrative structures and the cities of Soissons, Reims and Paris, which became his capital. The extent and nature of Syagrius's realm are debated: some see it as a substantial Roman state, others as a modest local lordship magnified by Gregory. Clovis's expansion from Tournai into the Roman heartland of northern Gaul made the Franks heirs to the provincial administration and the Gallo-Roman church, paving the way for his conversion and the battle of Vouillé.
set.debate: Gregory's date (Clovis's fifth year, 486 or 487) depends on an uncertain chronology; the 'kingdom of Soissons' may be largely a literary construct.

set.detail: Theodoric entered Italy in 489 as Zeno's agent against Odoacer and won battles on the Isonzo and at Verona. In 490 Odoacer's general Tufa defected and then returned to him; Odoacer retook Milan and besieged Theodoric in Pavia, but with Visigothic help Theodoric won on the Adda on 11 August 490 and blockaded Odoacer in Ravenna. The city, protected by marshes and lagoons, was nearly impregnable from land. A night sortie by Odoacer's Heruli on 10 July 491 against Theodoric's camp in the Pineta, the pine woods near Classe, was repulsed with heavy losses. From August 492 Theodoric used ships from Rimini to blockade the port of Classe, cutting supplies, and famine struck the city, where a modius of wheat cost six solidi. On 25 February 493, through the mediation of Bishop John of Ravenna, the two kings agreed to share rule over Italy; Odoacer handed over his son Thela as a hostage, and Theodoric entered Ravenna on 5 March. Ten days later, on 15 March, Theodoric killed Odoacer with his own hands at a banquet in the palace of the Laurel, cutting him from collarbone to hip, and said, according to John of Antioch, 'there was not a bone in this wretched man'. Theodoric justified the act by claiming that Odoacer had plotted against him. Odoacer's brother, wife and son were also killed, and his soldiers massacred throughout Italy. Theodoric then took the title of king (rex) and ruled Italy for 33 years, nominally as Zeno's representative. The siege established the Ostrogothic kingdom and made Ravenna the Gothic capital, the setting of Theodoric's great building programme.

scholarship: Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)

set.detail: Zeno died on 9 April 491 without a son, his only son Leo II having died in 474 and his other son Zeno before him. His brother Longinus, consul in 486 and 490, hoped to succeed. The ceremony book of Constantine VII preserves, from the sixth-century official Peter the Patrician, a detailed account of the selection. The high officials and the Senate, meeting in the palace, agreed with the patriarch Euphemius to let the empress Ariadne choose. The people in the Hippodrome chanted 'an orthodox emperor for the world' and 'a Roman emperor', a rejection of another Isaurian. Ariadne chose Anastasius, a silentiarius of about sixty from Dyrrachium, known for his piety and his miaphysite sympathies, whom she married on 20 May. Before his coronation on 11 April, Euphemius made him sign a written promise not to alter the faith of Chalcedon. Anastasius was crowned in the Hippodrome, appearing in the kathisma, raised on a shield, crowned with a torque by a military officer, then given the diadem by the patriarch. Anastasius's reign of 27 years was one of the most successful in eastern Roman history. He expelled the Isaurians from the capital and fought the Isaurian war of 492-497, reformed the copper coinage (498), abolished the chrysargyron tax on trade, replaced compulsory deliveries with cash payment (coemptio), and left a reserve of 320,000 lb of gold in the treasury. But his miaphysite sympathies caused riots in Constantinople (512) and the revolt of Vitalian (513-515). His accession ceremony is the first for which a detailed protocol survives.

scholarship: Haarer, Anastasius I: Politics and Empire in the Late Roman World (2006)

set.detail: Clovis, king of the Franks, had married around 493 the Burgundian princess Clotilde, a Catholic, while most Germanic rulers, including her own uncle Gundobad, were Arians. Gregory of Tours tells that Clotilde urged him to convert and that their first son, baptised, died, confirming Clovis's suspicion of her god. During a battle against the Alamanni, traditionally at Tolbiac (Zülpich), facing defeat, Clovis prayed to the god of Clotilde and promised to be baptised if he won. He won, and was instructed by Bishop Remigius of Reims and baptised with more than 3,000 of his warriors on a Christmas Day; Remigius told him 'bow your head, proud Sicambrian; adore what you have burned and burn what you have adored'. Gregory places the baptism in 496, after Clovis's fifth year, but the chronology is uncertain. A letter from Avitus of Vienne congratulating Clovis, which mentions his sister's conversion from Arianism, has led many scholars to place the baptism around 508, after Vouillé, and possibly at Tours. Others argue for c. 500 or 503. There is also debate whether Clovis was first attracted to Arianism, as his sister Lantechild had been. Whatever the date, the choice of Catholic over Arian Christianity was momentous. It allied the Franks with the Gallo-Roman bishops and aristocracy, who controlled the cities, and set them apart from the Arian Goths and Burgundians. Gregory presents Clovis as a new Constantine, and the Vouillé campaign as a crusade against heretics. The Franks became the main Catholic power of the West and later allies of the papacy. Later tradition invented the Holy Ampulla brought by a dove for the anointing, used at French coronations until 1825.
set.debate: Date debated: 496 (Gregory), c. 500, or 508 (from Avitus's letter).

scholarship: Wood, 'Gregory of Tours and Clovis', Revue belge de philologie et d'histoire 63 (1985)
Shanzer, 'Dating the baptism of Clovis', Early Medieval Europe 7 (1998)

set.detail: By 506 Clovis, ruler of northern Gaul, and Alaric II, king of the Visigoths of Toulouse, faced each other across the Loire. Theodoric, who was married to Clovis's sister Audofleda and whose daughter Theodegotha was Alaric's wife, wrote letters, preserved in Cassiodorus's Variae, urging both to keep the peace and appealing to the kings of the Burgundians, Heruli, Warni and Thuringians to join a coalition against aggression. Alaric tried to win his Catholic subjects with the Breviary (506) and the Council of Agde. In 507 Clovis, with the support of the Burgundians under Gundobad's son Sigismund and of Anastasius, who sent a fleet to raid southern Italy and prevent Theodoric's intervention, attacked. Gregory of Tours presents the campaign as a holy war against Arian heretics: Clovis said 'it grieves me that these Arians hold part of Gaul'. The armies met at the Campus Vogladensis, ten miles from Poitiers, in spring or summer 507. The Visigoths were defeated and Clovis killed Alaric with his own hand; Gregory adds that Clovis was saved from two Gothic spearmen by his armour and his horse. The Arvernian contingent, led by Sidonius Apollinaris's son Apollinaris, fought on the Visigothic side. Clovis wintered in Bordeaux and took the treasure at Toulouse in 508. The Visigoths lost all of Gaul except Septimania, which Theodoric's army saved in 508 by relieving Arles, and the Visigothic kingdom moved its centre to Spain, eventually at Toledo. The site of the battle is debated, with candidates including Vouillé and Voulon. In 508 Clovis received from Anastasius an honorary consulship at Tours. The victory made the Franks the dominant power in Gaul.
set.debate: The site (Vouillé or Voulon) and the role of Byzantine diplomacy are debated.

scholarship: Mathisen and Shanzer (eds.), The Battle of Vouillé, 507 CE (2012)

set.detail: Anastasius died on the night of 9-10 July 518, aged about 88, without having designated a successor, although his nephews Hypatius, Pompeius and Probus were well placed. The account in Constantine VII's De Ceremoniis, derived from Peter the Patrician, describes the confusion of the following day. In the Hippodrome the people waited while the senators and officials deliberated in the palace. The excubitors proposed a tribune named John, who was rejected by the Blues; the scholarians proposed the general Patricius, who was nearly killed by the excubitors. Justin, commander of the excubitors, an elderly illiterate Thracian peasant from Bederiana near Naissus who had come to Constantinople as a young man and risen through the guard, was finally accepted by the Senate and the army. Evagrius and Procopius allege that the grand chamberlain Amantius gave Justin money to buy the votes of the guards for his own candidate, Theocritus, and that Justin used it for himself. Justin was crowned in the Hippodrome, raised on a shield and crowned with a torque before the patriarch John placed the diadem on his head. His reign marked a decisive change in religious policy: within days crowds in Hagia Sophia demanded the proclamation of Chalcedon, and in 519 Justin ended the Acacian schism with Rome on the terms of Pope Hormisdas. Amantius and Theocritus were executed. Vitalian was recalled and made consul, then murdered in 520, probably on the orders of Justin's nephew Justinian, who became the real power in government. Procopius's Secret History mocks Justin as illiterate, signing documents with a stencil, a story often doubted.

Theodoric died at Ravenna on 30 August 526, after a reign of 33 years in Italy, the last few marked by crisis. The end of the Acacian schism in 519 removed the religious barrier between the Roman Senate and Constantinople and weakened the Arian king's position; the accusations of treasonable correspondence with the eastern court led to the executions of Boethius in 524 and Symmachus in 525. In 523 the Vandal king Hilderic had broken with Theodoric's sister Amalafrida and killed her Gothic guard, and in 525-526 Justin's anti-Arian measures in the East led Theodoric to send Pope John I to Constantinople, who died in prison on his return. The Anonymus Valesianus says that Theodoric had just ordered that Arians should take over Catholic churches when he died of dysentery, a divine judgement in the Catholic author's view; Procopius tells that he was served a large fish head at dinner, which he saw as the face of Symmachus threatening him, and died of the shock and grief. The succession was difficult. His only son-in-law and intended heir, Eutharic, had died in 522 or 523, and the throne passed to his ten-year-old grandson Athalaric under the regency of Theodoric's daughter Amalasuntha. Theodoric was buried in the mausoleum he had built outside the walls of Ravenna, with its 230-tonne monolithic dome; his remains were later removed, perhaps after the Byzantine reconquest. In Germanic legend he became Dietrich von Bern (Verona). Historians see his reign as a successful attempt to preserve Roman government and culture in Italy alongside a Gothic army, a balance that his death dissolved.

scholarship: Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)

set.detail: Justinian, born Petrus Sabbatius around 482 at Tauresium near Bederiana in Dardania, was the nephew of Justin I, who brought him to Constantinople and had him educated. During his uncle's reign he held the posts of comes domesticorum and magister militum praesentalis, was consul in 521, when he gave spectacular games, and was made nobilissimus and Caesar. He married Theodora, a former actress, around 525, after Justin changed the law forbidding senators to marry actresses. On 1 April 527 the aged and sick Justin crowned him co-emperor, and Theodora Augusta, in the palace; when Justin died on 1 August 527 Justinian became sole ruler. His reign of 38 years transformed the empire. In law, he commissioned the Code (529, 534), the Digest and Institutes (533) and issued the Novels. In war, his generals Belisarius and Narses reconquered Africa from the Vandals (533-534), Italy from the Ostrogoths (535-554) and part of southern Spain (552), while the Persian wars (527-532, 540-562) and Balkan invasions strained resources. In building, he rebuilt Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots, and Procopius's Buildings lists hundreds of churches, forts and aqueducts. In religion, he sought to unify Chalcedonians and Miaphysites, condemning the Three Chapters in 553, and persecuted pagans, heretics and Samaritans. His administration, through ministers such as John the Cappadocian and Tribonian, increased tax efficiency at the cost of popular hatred. The plague of 541-542 struck in the middle of his reign. Historians differ in assessing whether his reconquests overextended the empire, leaving his successors with an impossible burden, or represented a feasible restoration of Roman power.

scholarship: Maas (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (2005)

set.detail: The Iberian war began in 526 over the Persian attempt to impose Zoroastrian practices on Iberia and the construction of Roman forts on the frontier. In June 530 a Persian army under Perozes (Firuz), the mirranes, marched on Dara, the fortress built by Anastasius in 505 near Nisibis. Belisarius, newly appointed magister militum per Orientem, and Hermogenes, magister officiorum, had some 25,000 men; the Persians had about 40,000, later reinforced to 50,000. Belisarius dug a complex system of trenches in front of the city walls, in the shape of a broken line with a recessed centre, with gaps for counter-attacks, positioning his infantry behind the central trench and cavalry on the wings, with Hunnic cavalry under Sunicas and Aigan at the angles, and a detachment of Heruli under Pharas hidden behind a hill on the left. On the first day there were skirmishes and single combats, including one in which the bath attendant Andreas killed two Persian champions. After an exchange of letters, the battle took place on the second day. The Persian right attacked the Roman left and was taken in the flank and rear by Pharas's Heruli; the Persian left, with the elite Immortals, pressed the Roman right but was cut in two by the Hunnic cavalry of Sunicas, who killed the Persian standard-bearer and commander Baresmanas. Some 5,000 Persians died. Procopius, who was present as Belisarius's secretary, gives the most detailed account of the battle in his Wars. Dara was the first major Roman victory over the Persians in generations, and showed the combination of fieldworks, missile cavalry and mobile reserves that characterised the sixth-century Roman army.

scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)
Syvänne, Military History of Late Rome 518-565 (2021)

set.detail: In spring 531 a Persian army of about 15,000 cavalry under Azarethes, with the Lakhmid king al-Mundhir III, crossed the Euphrates at Circesium and advanced northward through Commagene, avoiding the fortified cities of Mesopotamia, to strike at Antioch. Belisarius, with some 20,000 men including the Ghassanid al-Harith and his Arabs, followed and forced them to retreat without battle. The Romans pursued them along the Euphrates. On 19 April 531, Easter Saturday, near Callinicum, Belisarius's troops, impatient for battle, forced their general to attack the Persians against his advice; Procopius says they insulted him, and that fasting soldiers were exhausted. Belisarius drew up his infantry on the left, near the river, with the Arabs on the right. The Persians, concentrating their best troops against the Arabs, broke the Roman right, the Arabs fleeing or, according to Procopius, betraying the Romans. The Roman cavalry fled, and Belisarius dismounted to join the infantry, which formed a shield wall with its back to the river and held until nightfall, when the survivors escaped across the Euphrates to an island and then to Callinicum. Malalas, who had access to the official report, gives a different version, less favourable to Belisarius, in which he fled across the river with his standard while the infantry fought on. A commission of inquiry under the magister militum Constantiolus found Belisarius at fault and he was recalled. Persian losses were also heavy, and Azarethes was disgraced by Kavad for failing to take any city. The battle led to peace negotiations, which were accelerated by Kavad's death later in 531 and concluded with the Eternal Peace in 532.
set.debate: Procopius's account exculpates Belisarius; Malalas, using the official report, is more critical.

scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)

set.detail: The circus factions, the Blues and the Greens, were organisations of fans and performers that had become powerful forces in urban politics across the empire. In January 532, after a riot, the urban prefect Eudaemon condemned several men to death; at the execution on 10 January the scaffold broke twice and two of the condemned, one Blue and one Green, survived and were taken by monks to sanctuary in the church of St Laurentius. At the races of 13 January, the factions asked Justinian for mercy, and when he did not respond, they united with the cry 'Nika' (conquer) and attacked the prefect's praetorium, freeing prisoners and setting fires. Over the following days the rioters burned the Chalke gate of the palace, the Senate house, the church of Hagia Sophia, the baths of Zeuxippus and much of the city centre, demanding the dismissal of John the Cappadocian, the praetorian prefect, Tribonian, the quaestor, and Eudaemon. Justinian dismissed them, but the rioters continued and on 18 January proclaimed Hypatius, nephew of Anastasius, emperor in the Hippodrome. Justinian considered fleeing by sea. Procopius puts into Theodora's mouth a speech arguing that 'royalty is a good burial shroud'. Belisarius and Mundus, with their bucellarii and Herul troops, entered the Hippodrome from two sides while the eunuch Narses bribed the Blues, and massacred the crowd: Procopius says over 30,000 were killed. Hypatius and his brother Pompeius were executed and their bodies thrown into the sea. The riots allowed Justinian to rebuild the city centre and Hagia Sophia, and strengthened his autocracy, as the factions and senatorial opposition were crushed. The ministers he had dismissed were reinstated.
set.debate: Theodora's speech is a Procopian literary construction; the death toll of 30,000-35,000 is a round figure.

scholarship: Greatrex, 'The Nika riot: a reappraisal', JHS 117 (1997)
Meier, 'Die Inszenierung einer Katastrophe: Justinian und der Nika-Aufstand', ZPE 142 (2003)

set.detail: The second church of Hagia Sophia, built by Theodosius II and dedicated in 415, was burned in the Nika riot on 14 January 532. Forty days later, on 23 February 532, Justinian began the construction of a new church on an unprecedented scale. Its designers were Anthemius of Tralles, a mathematician and author of a treatise on burning mirrors, and Isidore of Miletus, a geometer who edited Archimedes; they were not builders in the conventional sense, but theorists of geometry and mechanics. The church combined the longitudinal basilica with a centralised domed structure: a dome of about 31 m in diameter, rising some 55 m above the floor, rested on four massive piers and pendentives, buttressed by two semi-domes to east and west and by smaller exedrae, creating a nave of about 70 by 75 m. A ring of forty windows at the base of the dome made it seem, in Procopius's words, to be suspended from heaven by a golden chain. Some 10,000 workmen are said to have been employed; materials included green marble from Thessaly, porphyry from Egypt, and columns from older buildings. The church was dedicated on 27 December 537, after less than six years, and Justinian is said to have exclaimed, according to a later legend, 'Solomon, I have outdone you'. The dome, too shallow, collapsed partly after earthquakes in 557, on 7 May 558, and was rebuilt higher by Isidore the Younger, the church being rededicated in 562, the occasion of Paul the Silentiary's Ekphrasis. Hagia Sophia remained the largest church in Christendom for nearly a thousand years and served as the model for Ottoman imperial mosques.

sources.a: Narratio de aedificatione templi S. Sophiae
sources.w: Narratio de aedificatione templi S. Sophiae

scholarship: Mainstone, Hagia Sophia: Architecture, Structure and Liturgy of Justinian's Great Church (1988)
Mark and Çakmak (eds.), Hagia Sophia from the Age of Justinian to the Present (1992)
Krautheimer, Early Christian and Byzantine Architecture (1986)

set.detail: After the first edition of the Code in 529, Justinian ordered on 15 December 530, by the constitution Deo auctore, a commission of sixteen under Tribonian, the quaestor, to compile an anthology of the writings of the classical jurists who had the ius respondendi, from the late Republic to the third century. The commission, which included the law professors Theophilus and Dorotheus, read some 2,000 books of 3 million lines and condensed them into 50 books with 9,123 excerpts and about 150,000 lines, an operation completed in three years. The Digest (Greek: Pandects) was published on 16 December 533 by the constitution Tanta (in Greek, Dedoken), and entered into force on 30 December. Ulpian provides about 40 per cent of the text, Paul 17 per cent, with Papinian, Gaius, Modestinus and others. The compilers were authorised to alter texts (interpolations) to bring them into line with current law, and modern scholarship has long debated the extent of these changes. In parallel, Tribonian, Theophilus and Dorotheus compiled the Institutes, an elementary textbook in four books based on the Institutes of Gaius, promulgated on 21 November 533 by the constitution Imperatoriam, and given the force of law. The constitution Omnem reorganised legal education in a five-year course based on the new texts. The Digest is the main source for classical Roman law, which would otherwise be largely lost. Rediscovered in Italy in the eleventh century through the Florentine manuscript (Littera Florentina), copied in the sixth century, it became the basis of legal education in the universities of medieval Europe and of the civil law systems of continental Europe and beyond.

scholarship: Humfress, 'Law and legal practice in the age of Justinian', in Maas (ed.), Cambridge Companion (2005)

set.detail: After the Eternal Peace of 532 freed the eastern army, Justinian decided to intervene in Africa, where Gelimer had deposed the pro-Roman Hilderic in 530. Procopius reports that the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian opposed the expedition, recalling the disaster of 468 and the cost and risk of a sea campaign far from home, and that the generals feared it; a bishop's dream promising victory and the prospect of restoring Catholics' rights persuaded the emperor. Revolts in the Vandal provinces helped: Godas, governor of Sardinia, rebelled and asked for Roman support, and Pudentius led a rising in Tripolitania. Gelimer sent his brother Tzazon with 5,000 men and 120 ships to Sardinia, weakening his forces in Africa. Belisarius sailed from Constantinople around the summer solstice of 533 with 10,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry including his bucellarii, 400 Heruli and 600 Hunnic horse archers, in 500 transport ships with 30,000 sailors and 92 warships, accompanied by his wife Antonina and by Procopius. The voyage was difficult: bread baked insufficiently on John the Cappadocian's orders went mouldy and killed 500 men, and Belisarius executed two Huns for murder at Abydos. The fleet stopped in Sicily, where Amalasuntha's government provided supplies and a market, and where Procopius learned in Syracuse that the Vandals were unaware of the expedition and that Gelimer was away at Hermione. The fleet landed at Caput Vada, about 200 km south of Carthage, in early September. Belisarius insisted on strict discipline toward the inhabitants, presenting the Romans as liberators. The campaign ended Vandal rule in less than a year.

scholarship: Hughes, Belisarius: The Last Roman General (2009)

set.detail: After landing at Caput Vada in early September 533, Belisarius marched north along the coast with the fleet following, reaching the tenth milestone from Carthage, Ad Decimum, on 13 September. Gelimer, who had executed Hilderic and his family on hearing of the landing, planned a three-pronged ambush: his brother Ammatas would attack from Carthage, his nephew Gibamund with 2,000 men from the west, and Gelimer himself from the rear. The plan failed through bad coordination. Ammatas, arriving early with a small force, ran into the Roman vanguard under John the Armenian, killed twelve of the best Romans, but was killed in turn, and his men fled. Gibamund's force was destroyed by the Hunnic horse archers on the left flank. Gelimer, advancing between the Roman columns, routed the Roman advance cavalry and was in a position to win, but on finding his brother's body he stopped to mourn and bury him, losing the moment. Belisarius rallied his troops and drove off the Vandals, who fled west toward Numidia. Procopius says that if Gelimer had pressed on, he would have destroyed the Roman army or seized Carthage and the fleet. On 15 September 533 Belisarius entered Carthage unopposed, ate the banquet that had been prepared for Gelimer in the palace, and ensured that the soldiers bought what they needed instead of looting. The Catholic clergy took over the churches of the city, and the fleet entered the harbour of Mandracium. The battle was won with Belisarius's cavalry and bucellarii alone, in confused fighting, and showed the importance of Hunnic horse archers in sixth-century warfare.

scholarship: Syvänne, Military History of Late Rome 518-565 (2021)

set.detail: After the defeat at Ad Decimum, Gelimer retired to Bulla Regia in Numidia, bribed Moorish and Punic peasants to kill Romans, and recalled his brother Tzazon, who had recovered Sardinia. Reinforced, the Vandals advanced on Carthage, cutting the aqueduct, and tried to suborn Belisarius's Hunnic allies. In mid-December 533 Belisarius marched out and met them at Tricamarum, about 30 km west of Carthage. Procopius's figures suggest the Vandals outnumbered the Romans; the Romans' infantry arrived late, and the battle was fought by cavalry alone. Gelimer ordered his men to fight only with swords. The Romans under John the Armenian crossed a stream that separated the armies and made three charges against the Vandal centre, where Tzazon was killed. The Vandal army broke; some 800 Vandals and fewer than 50 Romans died. In the evening the Roman infantry attacked the Vandal camp, and Gelimer fled on horseback toward Numidia without warning his men, who abandoned the camp with its women, children and treasure. The Roman soldiers spent the night plundering, and Belisarius feared that a counter-attack would destroy his scattered army. Gelimer took refuge on Mount Papua among the Moors, where he was besieged by the Herul Pharas, and surrendered in March 534, reportedly asking for a lyre to accompany a song on his misfortune, a sponge to wipe his eyes and a loaf of bread. The Vandal treasure, including the vessels of the Temple of Jerusalem taken from Rome in 455, was seized at Hippo. Tricamarum completed the destruction of the Vandal kingdom after only three months, an extraordinary success that encouraged Justinian's further ambitions in Italy.

Amalasuntha, Theodoric's daughter, educated in Latin and Greek, governed Italy as regent for her son Athalaric from 526. Her Roman-style education of her son and her pro-imperial policy, including support for Belisarius's Vandal expedition in 533, alienated the Gothic nobles, who took Athalaric from her tutors and encouraged him in drinking; three leaders of the opposition were killed on her orders, and she secretly negotiated with Justinian for asylum in Constantinople, sending treasure to Dyrrachium. Athalaric died on 2 October 534, aged about 18. Amalasuntha made her cousin Theodahad, a wealthy landowner in Tuscia with philosophical interests, co-ruler, having him swear to leave government to her. Theodahad allied with the relatives of the murdered Gothic nobles, confined Amalasuntha on the island of Martana in Lake Bolsena and, in late April or early May 535, she was strangled in her bath. Procopius in the Wars attributes the murder to the relatives of the executed nobles with Theodahad's consent; in the Secret History he adds that Theodora, jealous of Amalasuntha's beauty and influence, had secretly instructed the imperial envoy Peter the Patrician to encourage the murder, a claim most scholars doubt. Justinian, whose envoy had promised protection, used the murder as a pretext for war. Belisarius occupied Sicily in late 535 and Mundus invaded Dalmatia, opening the Gothic war. Amalasuntha's letters in Cassiodorus's Variae show a ruler of great intelligence, whose fate illustrates the difficulty of maintaining the balance between Gothic military elite and Roman administration that Theodoric had achieved, and her murder gave Constantinople the moral pretext it had been waiting for.
set.debate: Theodora's involvement (Secret History 16) is generally doubted.

scholarship: Vitiello, Amalasuintha: The Transformation of Queenship in the Post-Roman World (2017)

set.detail: Procopius, in Africa or Italy, wrote that in 536 'the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon, during this whole year, and it seemed exceedingly like the sun in eclipse'. Cassiodorus, praetorian prefect in Italy, described a bluish sun, moonlight without lustre, a summer without heat, and frosts during harvest, and ordered the distribution of reserves. John Lydus in Constantinople reported a dimmed sun for almost a year; Michael the Syrian, drawing on John of Ephesus, says the sun was darkened for eighteen months, appearing for only four hours a day. Chinese chronicles record yellow dust and summer snow. Tree-ring evidence from Europe, Siberia and North America shows the coldest decade of the last two thousand years beginning in 536, with summer temperatures in the northern hemisphere 1.5-2.5 °C lower than average. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica reveal sulphate deposits, and a study published in 2018 by McCormick and others identified volcanic glass in a Swiss glacier core pointing to an Icelandic eruption in early 536, followed by another major eruption in 539-540, perhaps in the tropics (Ilopango in El Salvador has been proposed). The resulting cooling, sometimes called the Late Antique Little Ice Age (536-660), coincided with crop failures and famines, and some historians link it to the spread of the Justinianic plague from 541 and to migrations in Eurasia. The causal connections remain debated; the volcanic dimming of 536 is, however, one of the best-documented climatic events of antiquity, and it illustrates the use of written sources with natural science data.
set.debate: The identification of the eruptions and the extent of their social consequences are debated.

scholarship: Büntgen et al., 'Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age', Nature Geoscience 9 (2016)

set.detail: Belisarius entered Rome on 9 December 536 with only some 5,000 men, as the Gothic garrison withdrew. In February or March 537 Witiges arrived with an army that Procopius puts at 150,000, certainly greatly exaggerated, and established seven fortified camps around the city, six on the left bank and one on the Campus Neronis. The Goths cut all fourteen aqueducts, ending the use of the baths and forcing Belisarius to install floating mills on the Tiber, driven by the river current, to grind grain. The siege lasted a year and nine days. The Goths launched a major assault on the eighteenth day with siege towers drawn by oxen, which Belisarius stopped by shooting the oxen; the most dangerous attacks came at the Praenestine gate (Vivarium) and the Mausoleum of Hadrian, where the defenders broke up the statues and threw them at the Goths. Belisarius used sorties of mounted archers to inflict losses on the Goths, who lacked horse archers, a tactical analysis Procopius explains. Hunger and plague afflicted both sides. Pope Silverius was deposed in March 537, accused of plotting to open the Asinarian gate. Reinforcements arrived in November 537, and the Roman cavalry under John, nephew of Vitalian, raided Picenum, threatening the Gothic families. A three-month truce in December 537 allowed the Romans to occupy Portus, Ostia and Albanum, and in March 538 Witiges, hearing that John had taken Ariminum, raised the siege and retreated, burning his camps; Belisarius attacked his troops crossing the Milvian bridge. The siege was the longest of the Gothic war and showed the decisive importance of the Aurelian Walls and Belisarius's leadership.
set.debate: The size of the Gothic army is greatly exaggerated by Procopius.

scholarship: Heather, Rome Resurgent: War and Empire in the Age of Justinian (2018)

set.detail: After the siege of Rome, the Romans divided their command between Belisarius and Narses, and the Goths took and destroyed Milan in 539 because of these quarrels. Narses was recalled and Belisarius took Fiesole and Auximum in 539, while the Frankish invasion of Theudebert ravaged Liguria. In late 539 Belisarius blockaded Witiges in Ravenna, the strongest city of Italy, protected by marshes, and sent troops to the Po to cut off grain supplies; a fire, perhaps caused by Roman agents and Witiges's own wife Matasuntha, destroyed the Gothic grain stores. Justinian, threatened by Persia, sent envoys offering generous terms: Witiges would keep Italy north of the Po and half the royal treasure. Belisarius refused to sign the treaty. The Goths, admiring Belisarius, then offered to make him emperor of the West if he would rule them; Belisarius pretended to accept, and in May 540 entered Ravenna with his army. Procopius, who entered with him, says that the Gothic women spat in their husbands' faces at the sight of the small Roman army. Belisarius took Witiges, Matasuntha, the Gothic nobles and the royal treasure to Constantinople, where Justinian displayed the treasure to the senators in the palace but refused Belisarius a triumph. The Goths north of the Po, who had not surrendered, chose Ildibad, nephew of the Visigothic king Theudis, as king, then Eraric, and in 541 Totila, who reconquered almost all Italy. The fall of Ravenna appeared to end the war, but the departure of Belisarius and the financial demands of the imperial administration under the logothete Alexander, known as 'Snips' (Psalidios), alienated the Italians and gave the Goths a second chance.

Khosrow I, who had agreed to the Eternal Peace in 532, was alarmed by Justinian's successes in Africa and Italy and received envoys from Witiges and the Armenians urging war. In spring 540 he crossed the Euphrates with a large army, taking advantage of the absence of Belisarius in Italy. He burned Sura, whose bishop's appeal he rejected, extorted ransoms from Hierapolis (2,000 lb of silver) and Beroea (Aleppo), where the people took refuge in the citadel, and arrived at Antioch in June. The patriarch Ephraim and the governor fled, and Justinian's cousin Germanus, sent with a small force, retreated after deciding the walls were not defensible. The city's young men and Blues and Greens fought bravely, but the Persians broke in through a weak point near the citadel on the hills. Antioch, the third city of the empire, was sacked and burned, except for the great church; its inhabitants were deported to Mesopotamia, where Khosrow founded a new city near Ctesiphon called Weh Antiok Khosrow, 'Khosrow's better Antioch', with a hippodrome and baths, known to the Arabs as al-Rumiya. Khosrow bathed in the Mediterranean at Seleucia Pieria and watched chariot races at Apamea, where he favoured the Greens because Justinian favoured the Blues. On his return he extorted money from Edessa and other cities, and broke the treaty again by besieging Dara. Justinian agreed to pay 5,000 lb of gold immediately and 500 lb a year. The sack ended the Eternal Peace, opened twenty years of war in Mesopotamia and Lazica, and was a severe blow to Justinian's prestige.

scholarship: Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Downey, A History of Antioch in Syria (1961)

set.detail: The plague first appeared at Pelusium on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta in July 541, apparently arriving from the Red Sea, and spread west to Alexandria and east to Gaza and Palestine. It reached Constantinople in spring 542 and raged for four months. Procopius, an eyewitness, describes the symptoms: sudden fever, buboes in the groin and armpits, delirium, coma and death within a few days, with black pustules in some cases; he says the death toll rose to 5,000 and then 10,000 a day, and the bodies were piled in the towers of the walls of Sycae across the Golden Horn and in ships. John of Ephesus, who travelled through Asia Minor during the epidemic, describes deserted villages and fields and officials counting 230,000 dead in the capital before giving up. Evagrius, who caught the disease as a child at Antioch, says it recurred in cycles, killing his wife, children and grandchildren. The emperor himself fell ill and recovered. The plague spread to Italy, Gaul, Spain, Britain and Ireland and to Persia, recurring about every 10-15 years until 749. DNA analysis of skeletons from Aschheim in Bavaria and other sites, published from 2013, confirmed that the disease was caused by Yersinia pestis, a strain distinct from that of the Black Death, originating in central Asia. Mortality is debated: older estimates of a quarter to a half of the Mediterranean population have been challenged by Mordechai, Eisenberg and others, who argue for a less catastrophic impact; others, like Harper and Sarris, maintain the plague was a demographic disaster that undermined Justinian's reconquests and the late Roman economy.
set.debate: The scale of mortality and economic consequences are vigorously debated.

scholarship: Little (ed.), Plague and the End of Antiquity (2007)
Mordechai and Eisenberg, 'Rejecting catastrophe', Past & Present 244 (2019)
Wagner et al., Lancet Infectious Diseases 14 (2014)

set.detail: Procopius of Caesarea, legal adviser to Belisarius and author of the official History of the Wars, wrote around 550, after Theodora's death in 548, a work he did not publish: the Anekdota (unpublished things), known as the Secret History. In it he says he would now tell the truth he could not write while those responsible were alive. It is a savage attack on Justinian and Theodora, as well as on Belisarius and his wife Antonina. Justinian is portrayed as a demon in human form, who walked at night without a head, and whose policies destroyed the population and wealth of the empire, through endless wars, confiscations, the debasement of laws and the persecution of heretics and pagans. Theodora is portrayed as a former actress and prostitute of insatiable sexual appetite, with lurid scenes of her theatrical performances, who manipulated her husband and persecuted her enemies. Belisarius is a cuckold dominated by Antonina. The work survived in a single family of manuscripts and was known in the tenth century to the Suda; it was first published in 1623 from a manuscript in the Vatican library and was long considered a forgery. Its relationship with the Wars and the Buildings, a panegyric of Justinian's construction works, poses the problem of Procopius's real view: modern scholars debate whether he was a classical, traditionalist opponent of the regime (Kaldellis), a man with a complex view (Cameron), or whether the work served a specific political purpose. Its precise factual details on the tax system and administration often confirm other sources, while its personal invective draws on the conventions of classical invective.
set.debate: The date (550 or 558-559) and purpose of the work are debated.

scholarship: Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)
Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea: Tyranny, History and Philosophy (2004)
Kaldellis, Prokopios: The Secret History with Related Texts (2010)

set.detail: After years of reverses in Italy under Totila, Justinian assembled a new army under the eunuch Narses, who was given lavish funds and recruited a large force including Lombards (5,500 sent by Audoin), Heruli, Gepids and Huns as well as Roman regiments, perhaps 20,000-30,000 men in all. Narses marched along the Adriatic coast, bypassing Gothic positions at Verona, reached Ravenna in June 552 and advanced along the Via Flaminia. Totila, waiting for reinforcements under Teia, met him at Busta Gallorum near Taginae (Gualdo Tadino) in the Apennines in late June or early July 552. Narses placed his dismounted Lombards and Heruli in the centre, with Roman infantry and 8,000 archers on foot on the wings, slightly advanced in a crescent, and cavalry in reserve, while a hill on his left flank was occupied by fifty men. Totila delayed the battle until his 2,000 reinforcements arrived, performing equestrian exercises with his weapons in front of the armies, dressed in gold-decorated armour. In the afternoon the Gothic cavalry charged the Roman centre, where it was caught by the archers on the wings and broke, and the fleeing horsemen threw the infantry into disorder. Some 6,000 Goths were killed. Totila was mortally wounded in the flight and died at Caprae; Procopius gives two versions of his death. His bloodstained clothes and jewelled hat were sent to Constantinople and laid at Justinian's feet. Narses then sent the unruly Lombards home and marched on Rome, which he took, the fifth capture of the city in the war. The Goths elected Teia, who made a last stand at Mons Lactarius.
set.debate: The location of Busta Gallorum and the date (late June or July 552) are debated.

scholarship: Rance, 'Narses and the battle of Taginae', Historia 54 (2005)

set.detail: After Totila's death at Taginae, the surviving Goths gathered at Pavia and elected Teia king. He massacred Roman senators and 300 child hostages, and tried to obtain help from the Franks. Learning that Narses was besieging his brother Aligern, who guarded the Gothic treasure at Cumae, Teia marched south, avoiding Roman forces by following the Adriatic coast, and crossed into Campania. Narses blockaded him on the river Draco (the Sarno), near Nuceria, where the two armies faced each other for two months, the Goths supplied by their fleet. When the Romans captured the fleet through the treachery of its commander, the Goths, short of supplies, retreated to Mons Lactarius (the Monti Lattari, near Vesuvius) and then attacked the Roman army in desperation in late October 552 (or early 553). The battle lasted two days. The Goths fought on foot in a deep phalanx. Teia fought in the front line, holding off the Romans with his shield, which he exchanged for a new one when it was full of javelins; at the twelfth exchange, as his chest was exposed for a moment, he was struck by a javelin and killed. The Romans displayed his head on a pole, but the Goths fought on until the next evening, when they negotiated to leave Italy with their property and to live in freedom under no Roman command. About 1,000 Goths under Indulf withdrew to Pavia; others submitted. Procopius closes his History of the Wars with this battle; Agathias takes up the story. Gothic resistance continued in a few northern cities until 562, and Aligern surrendered Cumae in 553, joining Narses against the Franks.
set.debate: Date (October 552 or early 553) is uncertain; Procopius's account of Teia's last fight is literary.

set.detail: In 553, after the defeat of the Goths, an army of Franks and Alamanni under two Alamannic brothers, Butilinus and Leutharis, dukes in the service of the Frankish king Theudebald, invaded Italy, claiming to support the Goths; Agathias gives a figure of 75,000, obviously inflated. They ravaged central Italy and divided at Samnium: Leutharis marched along the Adriatic and into Apulia and Calabria; Butilinus marched along the Tyrrhenian coast as far as the Straits of Messina, sacking churches. Leutharis decided to return home with his booty, but his army was defeated near Fanum by the Armenian Artabanes, lost much of the plunder, and was decimated by plague in Venetia, where Leutharis died. Butilinus, whose men were dying of dysentery from eating unripe grapes, decided to fight Narses, and fortified a camp near Casilinum on the Volturnus in autumn 554. Narses, with some 18,000 men, drew up his infantry in the centre with the Heruli, and cavalry on the wings. The Franks, fighting on foot with throwing axes (francisca) and barbed spears (angons), attacked in a wedge, broke through the Roman centre where the Heruli were absent after a dispute, but were then caught by the Roman cavalry on both flanks, who shot them with arrows from horseback without engaging in close combat. Agathias claims only five of the Franks survived while the Romans lost 80 men. The victory, described by Agathias in detail, secured Italy against the Franks and allowed Narses to celebrate a triumph in Rome. It is a classic example of the effectiveness of mounted archers against heavy infantry, and Agathias's description of Frankish weapons is valuable for archaeology.
set.debate: Agathias's casualty figures are impossible; the role of the Heruli is disputed.

set.detail: Justinian died in the night of 14 to 15 November 565, aged about 83, after a reign of 38 years. In his last years he had devoted himself to theology, and his last edict, on the incorruptibility of the body of Christ (aphthartodocetism), had led to the deposition of the patriarch Eutychius in January 565 and resistance from the bishops; he died, Evagrius says, before it could be enforced. He had outlived Theodora (d. 548), Belisarius (d. March 565), Tribonian and John the Cappadocian, and he did not designate a successor. His nephew Justin, the curopalates, married to Theodora's niece Sophia, was in the palace and was informed by the praepositus Callinicus, who said the dying emperor had named him; with the support of the Senate and the excubitors under Tiberius, Justin was crowned on 15 November before his cousin Justin, son of Germanus, commanding on the Danube, could intervene. The poet Corippus, in his panegyric In laudem Iustini, describes Justinian's funeral: the emperor's body laid out on a golden bed in the palace, covered with a shroud embroidered by Sophia showing the victories of his reign, including the defeated Gelimer, and the procession to the church of the Holy Apostles, where he was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus in the mausoleum of Constantine. His legacy was mixed: he had reconquered Africa, Italy and part of Spain, codified Roman law and built Hagia Sophia, but left an exhausted treasury, an empire weakened by plague, the Balkans exposed to Avars and Slavs, and an unresolved religious division. Justin II's refusal to pay subsidies reflected this situation.

scholarship: Cameron, Flavius Cresconius Corippus: In laudem Iustini Augusti minoris (1976)
